blocks.md: **I solve ONE part now; a smaller me handles the rest. Plus a smallest case answered directly.**

Two questions design ANY recursion: (1) What is the SMALLEST input I can answer instantly? (base) (2) Given the answer for n−1, how do I build the answer for n? (leap). Write those two lines and the function writes itself.

items.title: Print 1..N and N..1
items.statement: Both orders using ONE function shape — move one line.
hints: Line before call vs after call.

solutionCode.label: one shape, one line moved

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the call stack.

followups.q: Why does moving one line reverse the order?
followups.a: The recursion always descends from n to 0 in the same order. What changes is when the work happens: before the call means the current frame acts first, so the outermost (largest) value is emitted first. After the call means every deeper frame finishes first, so the innermost (smallest) is emitted first and the stack unwinds in reverse.

followups.q: Which one is the tail call?
followups.a: The descending version — the recursive call is the last thing it does, so a compiler could turn it into a loop. The ascending version has work pending after the call, so its frame must survive. That is exactly why "do it on the unwind" costs real stack and "do it on the way down" need not.

solutionCode.label: return my part plus whatever recursion returns

followups.q: Why is the base `n <= 0` rather than `n == 0`?
followups.a: Defence against a negative argument. With `== 0`, calling sum_first_n(-1) recurses forever into more negative numbers until the stack dies. The `<=` makes the function total — it returns 0 for any non-positive input instead of crashing.

followups.q: Closed form?
followups.a: n(n+1)/2, computable in O(1). The recursion is a teaching device here — never ship an O(n) stack walk when a formula exists. Knowing which recursions have closed forms is worth as much as writing them.

items.title: Factorial Recursive
items.statement: n! with long long; note growth explosion.
hints: Multiply on unwind or wind, both valid.

solutionCode.label: linear fold with a product

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) stack. The VALUE explodes: 20! is the last factorial that fits in a signed 64-bit integer.

followups.q: Wind or unwind — does it matter?
followups.a: Not for the result. Multiplying on the way down (passing an accumulator) or on the way up (returning a product) both give n!. The accumulator version is tail-recursive and can be a loop; the returning version cannot. Choose based on whether you need the stack, not on the arithmetic.

followups.q: Where exactly does int64 break?
followups.a: 20! = 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 fits under the 9.22×10^18 ceiling. 21! = 5.1×10^19 does not — it wraps silently to a negative number with no warning. If n can exceed 20, you need big integers, a modulus, or logarithms.

items.title: Nth Fibonacci (naive)
items.statement: Implement; print call-count counter to SEE explosion at n=25.

solutionCode.label: branching tree with a call counter to make the explosion visible
solutionCode.py:
def fib_with_count(n: int) -> tuple:
    """Returns (value, call_count) so the explosion is measurable, not asserted."""
    calls = 0

    def rec(k):
        nonlocal calls
        calls += 1                 # count EVERY invocation
        if k <= 1:
            return k
        return rec(k - 1) + rec(k - 2)   # two branches: the tree doubles

    val = rec(n)
    return val, calls
# n=15 -> 1973 calls; n=25 -> 242785 calls; n=40 -> ~331 million.

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) — nearly every call spawns two more. Space O(n) stack depth. Memoisation collapses it to O(n).

followups.q: Why 2^n and not n^2?
followups.a: Each call makes two more, so level d of the tree holds about 2^d nodes and the tree is n deep. The total is the sum of a geometric series, dominated by its last term — roughly 2^n. The exact count is 2*fib(n+1) - 1, which grows at phi^n ~ 1.618^n.

followups.q: What makes memoisation collapse it?
followups.a: The tree recomputes the same subproblems constantly — fib(n-2) appears in both branches. Caching each result means each of the n distinct values is computed once, so the tree becomes a path: O(n) time, O(n) space. That single observation is the entire bridge into dynamic programming.

items.title: Reverse Array Recursively

solutionCode.label: swap the ends, recurse inward

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) stack. The iterative two-pointer version is O(1) space.

followups.q: Why `l >= r` and not `l == r`?
followups.a: On an even-length array the pointers cross without ever being equal — l becomes r+1. With `==` the base never fires and the recursion runs off both ends. `>=` catches both the odd case (they meet) and the even case (they cross).

followups.q: Is recursion worth it here?
followups.a: No. It is O(n) stack to do what a while loop does in O(1), and at n = 10^5 it blows the stack. This exists to show that a two-pointer loop and a shrinking recursion are the same algorithm — useful framing, not a shippable implementation.

solutionCode.label: compare the ends, shrink inward

followups.q: Why does the empty string return True?
followups.a: l starts at 0 and r at -1, so `l >= r` fires immediately. That is the correct convention — a string with no characters reads the same in both directions vacuously. It falls out of the base case rather than needing a guard.

followups.q: Where does the early exit save work?
followups.a: On a mismatch at the very first pair, the function returns after one comparison instead of walking to the middle. Worst case (a true palindrome) is still n/2 frames, but the average on random input is a couple of frames — the `return false` is doing real work, not just tidiness.

items.title: Power (recursive halving)
items.statement: Archetype #4; explain why NOT b*power(b,e-1) linear.

solutionCode.label: square the base, halve the exponent

items.complexity: Halving: O(log e) multiplications. Linear: O(e). At e = 10^9 that is 30 versus a billion.

followups.q: Why store `half` instead of writing powFast(b,e/2) * powFast(b,e/2)?
followups.a: Writing it twice makes two recursive calls, so the recurrence becomes T(e) = 2T(e/2) + O(1) — which solves to O(e), exactly as slow as the linear version. Storing the result makes it T(e) = T(e/2) + O(1) = O(log e). One variable is the entire difference.

followups.q: Why does the odd case need the extra multiply?
followups.a: Integer division truncates: for odd e, e/2 rounds down, so half*half gives b^(e-1). Multiplying by b once restores b^e. Forgetting it produces an answer that is off by a factor of b on exactly the odd exponents.

items.title: Sum of Digits Recursive

solutionCode.label: peel the last digit, recurse on the rest

items.complexity: Time O(number of digits) = O(log n). Space O(log n) stack.

followups.q: What does this return for n = 0?
followups.a: 0, from the base case — which is correct, since the digit 0 sums to 0. The coincidence that "no digits left" and "the digit zero" give the same answer is why this one needs no special case, unlike R109 where the two differ.

followups.q: Why take abs() first?
followups.a: In C++, -123 % 10 is -3, so the sum comes out negative. In Python, -123 % 10 is 7 — a different wrong answer. Neither is what "sum of digits" means. Normalising the sign once at the top makes the behaviour identical in both languages.

items.title: Count Zeros in Number
items.statement: Count zero digits recursively (careful n=0 itself).
hints: Base distinction: n==0 → 1 vs general stop at 0 via n==0 return 0 with separate guard.

solutionCode.label: convention stated first, then enforced by a wrapper

items.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n) stack.

followups.q: Why does this need a wrapper when R108 did not?
followups.a: Because two different meanings collide on the same value. For digit-sum, "no digits left" and "the digit 0" both contribute 0, so one base case serves both. For zero-counting they differ: nothing left contributes 0, but the digit zero contributes 1. Separating them into a wrapper and a helper is the only clean fix.

followups.q: What if the interviewer wants countZeros(0) == 0?
followups.a: Then drop the wrapper and use the helper directly. Either convention is defensible — what is not defensible is failing to notice the ambiguity. State your choice before writing the code and the answer is correct either way.

items.title: Check Sorted Array Recursively

solutionCode.label: pairwise check, short-circuit on the first violation

items.complexity: Time O(n) worst case with early exit, space O(n) stack.

followups.q: What does the short-circuit actually save?
followups.a: Every frame below the violation. On [5,1,2,3,...,10^5] the check fails at i=0 and the function returns after one comparison — no stack growth at all. Without short-circuiting you would evaluate the full recursion and then AND the results, costing O(n) frames to learn something known at step one.

followups.q: Why does the base handle the empty array correctly?
followups.a: For an empty list, len(a) - 1 is -1, and i starts at 0, so `0 >= -1` fires immediately and returns True. An empty sequence is vacuously sorted. Writing the base as `i == len(a) - 1` would miss it and index out of bounds.

revisionCard: Design = two lines: instant-smallest base + one-part-plus-leap
Before-call = downward order · after-call = unwind order
Branching recursion explodes exponentially when subproblems overlap
Leap of faith: assume smaller answer correct
Halving-power beats linear power (same DNA as binary exponentiation)
Stack depth = longest chain — watch inputs
